# Product support — an ontology-v1 recipe template.
#
# Tickets, call transcripts, a feedback board, release notes. The questions it
# is built to answer: how many customers asked for a feature this quarter;
# which features come up in churn conversations; which issues a release
# resolved. The declaration is ONTOLOGY_PRIMITIVES.md §1.10 verbatim, plus
# the `organization` and `feature` types its facets point at.
#
# Scaffold:  svrn recipe new --ontology product-support --id my-support --out my-support.toml
# Then fill the REPLACE_ME fields, and:
#   svrn recipe validate my-support.toml     # prints what the ontology derives
#   svrn corpus install my-support.toml
#   svrn enrich init my-support --from-corpus my-support
#   svrn enrich build my-support --full

[corpus]
# REQUIRED: a stable, repo-scoped id.
id = "uv-support"
# REQUIRED: human-readable name.
name = "uv-support"
description = "Tickets, transcripts, feedback and release notes, extracted as customers, features and the requests customers make, with sentiment."
license = "private"
mesh_sharing = false
schema_version = 1

# One markdown file: each ticket, transcript, board post and release note as
# a `## ` section (dates in the headings let requests be counted by quarter).
[acquire]
type = "local_file"
# REQUIRED: the source file — an absolute path, or one relative to this recipe.
path = "REPLACE_ME"

[extract]
type = "markdown"

[chunk]
type = "paragraph"
max_chars = 2000
overlap_chars = 200

[index]
fts = true
vector = true

[enrichment]
enabled = true
type = "atlas"
domain = "product-support"

[enrichment.ontology]
version = 1
guidance = """
This corpus is a product's support record: tickets, call transcripts, a feedback board
and release notes. Customers are organizations known by account id. A request is a
customer asking for something of a feature — offline mode, an export, a fix — with the
sentiment it was made in; the same customer asking for the same thing twice is one
request. Release notes say which issues a version resolved.
"""

[[enrichment.ontology.types]]
name = "organization"
kind = "entity"
description = "A company or team that holds an account."

[[enrichment.ontology.types]]
name = "customer"
kind = "entity"
role_of = "organization"
identity = ["account_id"]

[[enrichment.ontology.types]]
name = "feature"
kind = "entity"
description = "A product capability customers ask about: offline mode, SSO, exports."

[[enrichment.ontology.types]]
name = "ticket"
kind = "event"
source = { file = "tickets.jsonl", attributes = { opened = "created_at", status = "status" } }

[[enrichment.ontology.types]]
name = "request"
kind = "claim"
force = "directive"
deontic = ["request"]
subject = "feature"
identity_fallback = ["subject", "customer"]
attributes = [{ name = "customer", type = "ref", of = "customer" }, { name = "sentiment", type = "text", values = ["positive", "neutral", "negative"] }]

# uv-support — the astral-sh/uv public issue tracker, as the real problems behind the reports.
#
# Source shape (assumed): a JSONL export of the tracker, one record per tracker item —
# an issue's opening post, each comment, and each timeline event (labeled, assigned,
# closed, reopened, marked as duplicate, cross-referenced by a pull request). Every
# record carries the issue it belongs to, so a thread is one issue:
#   { "id": "...", "issue_number": "1234", "item": "comment", "title": "...",
#     "body": "...", "author": "login", "author_association": "MEMBER",
#     "created_at": "2025-03-01T12:00:00Z" }
# Timeline events are rendered to a sentence in `body` ("charliermarsh closed this as
# completed in #1250").

[corpus]
id = "uv-support"
name = "uv issue tracker (astral-sh/uv)"
description = "Issues, comments and maintainer actions on the uv issue tracker, extracted as the underlying problems behind reports: which reports are the same problem, what each problem is, where it shows up, where it stands and what was decided or shipped."
license = "private"
mesh_sharing = false
schema_version = 1

[acquire]
type = "local_file"
path = "SOURCE_PATH"

[extract]
type = "jsonl"
content_field = "body"
title_field = "title"

[chunk]
type = "paragraph"
max_chars = 2000
overlap_chars = 200

[index]
fts = true
vector = true

[enrichment]
enabled = true
type = "atlas"
domain = "uv-issue-tracker"

[enrichment.ontology]
version = 1
guidance = """
This is the public issue tracker of uv, the Python package and project manager Astral
builds in Rust. People open issues about crashes, wrong resolutions, slow installs,
platform quirks, how a command should behave, and features they want; maintainers label,
assign, link pull requests, close, reopen and mark duplicates. Many issues report the same
underlying problem in different words, on different uv versions, operating systems and
Python versions. Keep the issue (a report, known by its number) apart from the problem
(the real defect, gap or misunderstanding behind one or more reports). A report can start
as a question and turn out to be a bug, or start as a bug and turn out to be a
misunderstanding: what a problem is, is what the latest maintainer diagnosis says. Record
where each problem was seen (uv version, OS, architecture, Python version), what
maintainers decided about it, and which pull request and release shipped the change.
Error messages, tracebacks and version strings quoted in reports are evidence, not prose.
"""
must_not = [
  "say a problem is fixed, or fixed in a release, unless a maintainer or a merged pull request says so",
  "present a reporter's guess at the cause as the maintainers' diagnosis",
  "treat an issue closed as a duplicate as a resolved problem",
]

# ── Shape: the things ─────────────────────────────────────────────

[[enrichment.ontology.types]]
name = "issue"
kind = "entity"
label = "issue"
description = "One report on the tracker, known by its number: a bug report, question, feature request or discussion as the reporter filed it."
attributes = [
  { name = "number", type = "text", description = "The GitHub issue number, digits only." },
  { name = "title", type = "text" },
  { name = "filed_as", type = "text", values = ["bug", "question", "feature-request", "documentation", "performance", "other"], description = "What the reporter filed it as, not what it turned out to be." },
  { name = "opened", type = "time" },
]
identity = ["number"]
source = { metadata = ["issue_number"], attributes = { number = "value" } }

[[enrichment.ontology.types]]
name = "problem"
kind = "entity"
label = "problem"
description = "The real problem behind one or more issues: a defect, regression, performance problem, platform quirk, missing feature, documentation gap, or a misunderstanding of intended behaviour."
attributes = [
  { name = "summary", type = "text", description = "What the problem actually is, in one sentence." },
  { name = "component", type = "ref", of = "component" },
  { name = "nature", type = "text", values = ["bug", "regression", "performance", "platform-specific", "upstream", "missing-feature", "documentation-gap", "intended-behaviour", "user-error"] },
  { name = "error_signature", type = "text", description = "The characteristic error message or failure, normalised (paths, versions and usernames removed)." },
]
identity_fallback = ["component", "error_signature"]
identity_criterion = "Two mentions are one problem when one change to uv (or one upstream fix) would resolve both: the same faulty behaviour of the same code path, however differently it was worded and whatever uv version, OS or Python version it was seen on. Same error message alone is not enough (one message can have several causes); different symptoms can be one problem when maintainers trace them to one cause. An issue marked as a duplicate of another reports the same problem."

[[enrichment.ontology.types]]
name = "component"
kind = "entity"
description = "A part of uv a problem lives in: the resolver, installer, Python discovery and downloads, lockfile, workspaces, the pip interface, tools, the cache, the build backend, publishing, configuration, or a specific command such as `uv sync` or `uv pip compile`."
attributes = [
  { name = "area", type = "text", values = ["resolver", "installer", "python-management", "lockfile", "projects-workspaces", "pip-interface", "tools", "cache", "build", "publish", "configuration", "cli"] },
  { name = "command", type = "text", description = "The uv command, when the component is one, e.g. `uv pip install`." },
]
identity_fallback = ["area", "command"]

[[enrichment.ontology.types]]
name = "package"
kind = "entity"
description = "A third-party Python package, index or build tool involved in a problem (torch, numpy, a private index, setuptools)."
attributes = [
  { name = "normalized_name", type = "text", description = "PEP 503 normalised name: lowercase, runs of -_. collapsed to -." },
]
identity = ["normalized_name"]

[[enrichment.ontology.types]]
name = "release"
kind = "entity"
description = "A uv release, known by its version (0.4.18, 0.5.0)."
attributes = [
  { name = "version", type = "text", description = "The version string without a leading v." },
  { name = "released", type = "time" },
]
identity = ["version"]

[[enrichment.ontology.types]]
name = "pull_request"
kind = "entity"
description = "A pull request on astral-sh/uv (or upstream) linked to an issue."
attributes = [

version = 1

This is the public issue tracker of uv, the Python package and project manager Astral
builds in Rust. People open issues about crashes, wrong resolutions, slow installs,
platform quirks, how a command should behave, and features they want; maintainers label,
assign, link pull requests, close, reopen and mark duplicates. Many issues report the same
underlying problem in different words, on different uv versions, operating systems and
Python versions. Keep the issue (a report, known by its number) apart from the problem
(the real defect, gap or misunderstanding behind one or more reports). A report can start
as a question and turn out to be a bug, or start as a bug and turn out to be a
misunderstanding: what a problem is, is what the latest maintainer diagnosis says. Record
where each problem was seen (uv version, OS, architecture, Python version), what
maintainers decided about it, and which pull request and release shipped the change.

kind = "entity"

identity = ["number"]
source = { metadata = ["issue_number"], attributes = { number = "value" } }

name = "problem"
kind = "entity"
label = "problem"
description = "The real problem behind one or more issues: a defect, regression, performance problem, platform quirk, missing feature, documentation gap, or a misunderstanding of intended behaviour."
attributes = [

# an issue's opening post, each comment, and each timeline event (labeled, assigned,
# closed, reopened, marked as duplicate, cross-referenced by a pull request). Every
# record carries the issue it belongs to, so a thread is one issue:
#   { "id": "...", "issue_number": "1234", "item": "comment", "title": "...",
#     "body": "...", "author": "login", "author_association": "MEMBER",

license = "private"

schema_version = 1

content_field = "body"

underlying problem in different words, on different uv versions, operating systems and

as a question and turn out to be a bug, or start as a bug and turn out to be a
misunderstanding: what a problem is, is what the latest maintainer diagnosis says. Record

guidance = """
This is the public issue tracker of uv, the Python package and project manager Astral
builds in Rust. People open issues about crashes, wrong resolutions, slow installs,
platform quirks, how a command should behave, and features they want; maintainers label,
assign, link pull requests, close, reopen and mark duplicates. Many issues report the same
underlying problem in different words, on different uv versions, operating systems and
Python versions. Keep the issue (a report, known by its number) apart from the problem
(the real defect, gap or misunderstanding behind one or more reports). A report can start
as a question and turn out to be a bug, or start as a bug and turn out to be a
misunderstanding: what a problem is, is what the latest maintainer diagnosis says. Record
where each problem was seen (uv version, OS, architecture, Python version), what
maintainers decided about it, and which pull request and release shipped the change.
Error messages, tracebacks and version strings quoted in reports are evidence, not prose.
"""
must_not = [
  "say a problem is fixed, or fixed in a release, unless a maintainer or a merged pull request says so",
  "present a reporter's guess at the cause as the maintainers' diagnosis",
  "treat an issue closed as a duplicate as a resolved problem",
]

kind = "entity"
label = "issue"

]

description = "The real problem behind one or more issues: a defect, regression, performance problem, platform quirk, missing feature, documentation gap, or a misunderstanding of intended behaviour."

[chunk]
type = "paragraph"
max_chars = 2000
overlap_chars = 200

[index]
fts = true
vector = true

[enrichment]
enabled = true
type = "atlas"
domain = "uv-issue-tracker"

[enrichment.ontology]
version = 1
guidance = """
This is the public issue tracker of uv, the Python package and project manager Astral
builds in Rust. People open issues about crashes, wrong resolutions, slow installs,
platform quirks, how a command should behave, and features they want; maintainers label,
assign, link pull requests, close, reopen and mark duplicates. Many issues report the same
underlying problem in different words, on different uv versions, operating systems and
Python versions. Keep the issue (a report, known by its number) apart from the problem
(the real defect, gap or misunderstanding behind one or more reports). A report can start
as a question and turn out to be a bug, or start as a bug and turn out to be a
misunderstanding: what a problem is, is what the latest maintainer diagnosis says. Record
where each problem was seen (uv version, OS, architecture, Python version), what
maintainers decided about it, and which pull request and release shipped the change.
Error messages, tracebacks and version strings quoted in reports are evidence, not prose.
"""
must_not = [
  "say a problem is fixed, or fixed in a release, unless a maintainer or a merged pull request says so",
  "present a reporter's guess at the cause as the maintainers' diagnosis",
  "treat an issue closed as a duplicate as a resolved problem",
]

# ── Shape: the things ─────────────────────────────────────────────

[[enrichment.ontology.types]]
name = "issue"
kind = "entity"
label = "issue"
description = "One report on the tracker, known by its number: a bug report, question, feature request or discussion as the reporter filed it."
attributes = [
  { name = "number", type = "text", description = "The GitHub issue number, digits only." },
  { name = "title", type = "text" },
  { name = "filed_as", type = "text", values = ["bug", "question", "feature-request", "documentation", "performance", "other"], description = "What the reporter filed it as, not what it turned out to be." },
  { name = "opened", type = "time" },
]
identity = ["number"]
source = { metadata = ["issue_number"], attributes = { number = "value" } }

[[enrichment.ontology.types]]
name = "problem"
kind = "entity"
label = "problem"
description = "The real problem behind one or more issues: a defect, regression, performance problem, platform quirk, missing feature, documentation gap, or a misunderstanding of intended behaviour."
attributes = [
  { name = "summary", type = "text", description = "What the problem actually is, in one sentence." },
  { name = "component", type = "ref", of = "component" },
  { name = "nature", type = "text", values = ["bug", "regression", "performance", "platform-specific", "upstream", "missing-feature", "documentation-gap", "intended-behaviour", "user-error"] },
  { name = "error_signature", type = "text", description = "The characteristic error message or failure, normalised (paths, versions and usernames removed)." },
]
identity_criterion = "Two mentions are one problem when one change to uv (or one upstream fix) would resolve both: the same faulty behaviour of the same code path, however differently it was worded and whatever uv version, OS or Python version it was seen on. Same error message alone is not enough (one message can have several causes); different symptoms can be one problem when maintainers trace them to one cause. An issue marked as a duplicate of another reports the same problem."

[[enrichment.ontology.types]]
name = "component"
kind = "entity"
description = "A part of uv a problem lives in: the resolver, installer, Python discovery and downloads, lockfile, workspaces, the pip interface, tools, the cache, the build backend, publishing, configuration, or a specific command such as `uv sync` or `uv pip compile`."
attributes = [
  { name = "area", type = "text", values = ["resolver", "installer", "python-management", "lockfile", "projects-workspaces", "pip-interface", "tools", "cache", "build", "publish", "configuration", "cli"] },
  { name = "command", type = "text", description = "The uv command, when the component is one, e.g. `uv pip install`." },
]
identity_fallback = ["area", "command"]

[[enrichment.ontology.types]]
name = "package"
kind = "entity"
description = "A third-party Python package, index or build tool involved in a problem (torch, numpy, a private index, setuptools)."
attributes = [
  { name = "normalized_name", type = "text", description = "PEP 503 normalised name: lowercase, runs of -_. collapsed to -." },
]
identity = ["normalized_name"]

[[enrichment.ontology.types]]
name = "release"
kind = "entity"
description = "A uv release, known by its version (0.4.18, 0.5.0)."
attributes = [
  { name = "version", type = "text", description = "The version string without a leading v." },
  { name = "released", type = "time" },
]
identity = ["version"]

[[enrichment.ontology.types]]
name = "pull_request"
kind = "entity"
description = "A pull request on astral-sh/uv (or upstream) linked to an issue."
attributes = [
  { name = "number", type = "text" },
  { name = "repository", type = "text", description = "owner/name; astral-sh/uv unless stated." },
  { name = "merged", type = "time" },
]
identity = ["repository", "number"]

[[enrichment.ontology.types]]
name = "github_user"
kind = "entity"
description = "A GitHub account that opened, commented on or acted on an issue."
attributes = [
  { name = "login", type = "text" },
]
identity = ["login"]
source = { metadata = ["author"], attributes = { login = "value" } }

[[enrichment.ontology.types]]
name = "maintainer"
kind = "entity"
role_of = "github_user"
description = "A uv maintainer or Astral team member acting on the tracker (author_association MEMBER or OWNER)."
attributes = [{ name = "login", type = "text" }]
identity = ["login"]

[[enrichment.ontology.types]]
name = "reporter"
kind = "entity"
role_of = "github_user"
description = "Someone who opened an issue or reported seeing the problem."

# ── Relations ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────

[[enrichment.ontology.types]]
name = "reports"
kind = "relation"
from = "issue"
to = "problem"
description = "The issue is a report of the problem."

[[enrichment.ontology.types]]
name = "duplicate_of"
kind = "relation"
from = "issue"
to = "issue"
description = "A maintainer marked the first issue a duplicate of the second."

[[enrichment.ontology.types]]
name = "addresses"
kind = "relation"
from = "pull_request"
to = "problem"
description = "The pull request fixes, works around or implements the problem."

[[enrichment.ontology.types]]
name = "shipped_in"
kind = "relation"
from = "pull_request"
to = "release"

[[enrichment.ontology.types]]
name = "involves"
kind = "relation"
from = "problem"
to = "package"
description = "The problem shows up with, or is caused by, this package or index."

# ── Events and states: how an issue got where it is ───────────────

[[enrichment.ontology.types]]
name = "triage_action"
kind = "event"
description = "Something a maintainer did to an issue: labeled, unlabeled, assigned, closed, reopened, marked duplicate, linked a pull request, transferred, locked."
participants = { actor = "maintainer", issue = "issue" }
attributes = [
  { name = "action", type = "text", values = ["labeled", "unlabeled", "assigned", "closed", "reopened", "marked-duplicate", "linked-pr", "transferred", "locked"] },
  { name = "label", type = "text", description = "The label added or removed, e.g. bug, needs-mre, question." },
  { name = "close_reason", type = "text", values = ["completed", "not-planned", "duplicate"] },
  { name = "at", type = "time" },
]

[[enrichment.ontology.types]]
name = "issue_state"
kind = "state"
of = "issue"
description = "Whether the issue is open or closed, and under which labels, over time."

[[enrichment.ontology.types]]
name = "problem_state"
kind = "state"
of = "problem"
description = "Where the problem stands: unconfirmed, confirmed, in progress, fixed, released, won't fix, upstream."

# ── Assertion: what the tracker says about problems ───────────────

[[enrichment.ontology.types]]
name = "diagnosis"
kind = "claim"
force = "assertive"
subject = "problem"
label = "diagnosis"
description = "What the problem actually is and why it happens. The latest maintainer diagnosis is what the problem is."
grades = ["fix-merged", "maintainer-reproduced", "maintainer-assessment", "reporter-reproduced", "reporter-speculation"]
attributes = [
  { name = "nature", type = "text", values = ["bug", "regression", "performance", "platform-specific", "upstream", "missing-feature", "documentation-gap", "intended-behaviour", "user-error"] },
  { name = "cause", type = "text", description = "The cause, as stated." },
  { name = "component", type = "ref", of = "component" },
  { name = "issue", type = "ref", of = "issue" },
]

[[enrichment.ontology.types]]
name = "occurrence"
kind = "claim"
force = "assertive"
subject = "problem"
label = "sighting"
description = "The problem was seen (or was not seen) in a given environment."
grades = ["maintainer-reproduced", "reporter-reproduced-minimal", "reporter-report", "hearsay"]
attributes = [
  { name = "issue", type = "ref", of = "issue" },
  { name = "uv_version", type = "ref", of = "release" },
  { name = "os", type = "text", values = ["linux", "macos", "windows", "freebsd", "other"] },
  { name = "os_detail", type = "text", description = "Distribution, version, libc (glibc/musl), WSL, Docker image." },
  { name = "arch", type = "text", values = ["x86_64", "aarch64", "i686", "other"] },
  { name = "python_version", type = "text", description = "e.g. 3.12.4, 3.13t, pypy3.10." },
  { name = "seen", type = "text", values = ["reproduces", "does-not-reproduce"] },
]

[[enrichment.ontology.types]]
name = "resolution"
kind = "claim"
force = "declaration"
subject = "problem"
label = "resolution"
description = "A maintainer settles where a problem stands: fixed, won't fix, by design, upstream, duplicate, needs reproduction, reopened."
attributes = [
  { name = "outcome", type = "text", values = ["fixed", "partially-fixed", "wont-fix", "intended-behaviour", "upstream", "duplicate", "needs-reproduction", "cannot-reproduce", "reopened", "stale"] },
  { name = "pull_request", type = "ref", of = "pull_request" },
  { name = "fixed_in", type = "ref", of = "release" },
  { name = "issue", type = "ref", of = "issue" },
]

[[enrichment.ontology.types]]
name = "behaviour_decision"
kind = "claim"
force = "declaration"
subject = "component"
label = "decision"
description = "A maintainer decides how a command or part of uv should behave (or that the current behaviour is intended), usually in answer to a question or feature request."
attributes = [
  { name = "decision", type = "text" },
  { name = "issue", type = "ref", of = "issue" },
  { name = "shipped_in", type = "ref", of = "release" },
]

[[enrichment.ontology.types]]
name = "feature_request"
kind = "claim"
force = "directive"
deontic = ["request"]
subject = "problem"
label = "request"
description = "Someone asks uv to do something it does not do."
attributes = [
  { name = "asked", type = "text" },
  { name = "issue", type = "ref", of = "issue" },
]

[[enrichment.ontology.types]]
name = "commitment"
kind = "claim"
force = "commissive"
subject = "problem"
description = "A maintainer undertakes something: will fix, plans for a release, would accept a pull request."
attributes = [
  { name = "undertaking", type = "text", values = ["will-fix", "planned", "pr-welcome", "investigating"] },
  { name = "target_release", type = "ref", of = "release" },
]

# ── Voices ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

[enrichment.ontology.voices]
not_entities = ["the reporter", "the commenter", "the original poster", "github-actions", "bot"]
attributed_to = ["maintainer", "reporter", "other-user", "bot"]

# ── Change: what holds when ──────────────────────────────────────

[enrichment.ontology.change]
supersedes = { diagnosis = "document_date", resolution = "document_date", behaviour_decision = "document_date", commitment = "document_date" }
document = { date = "created_at", thread = "issue_number", id = "id" }

# ── Derivation: what no single comment says ──────────────────────

[enrichment.ontology.tension]
label = "conflict"
between = ["diagnosis", "occurrence", "resolution", "behaviour_decision"]
same = ["subject"]
not_conflicts = [
  "A problem that reproduces on one OS, architecture or Python version and not on another is a platform-specific problem, not a contradiction.",
  "A report filed as a question and later diagnosed as a bug (or the reverse) is a reclassification; the later maintainer diagnosis replaces the earlier one.",
  "A problem seen on a uv version older than the release that fixed it is consistent with the fix.",
  "An issue closed as a duplicate while the problem stays open is not a resolution of the problem.",
  "A reporter's guess at a cause that a maintainer later corrects is superseded, not in conflict.",
]

[[enrichment.ontology.patterns]]
type = "circular_flow"
name = "duplicate_cycles"
description = "Issues marked duplicates of each other in a cycle, so no issue is the canonical one."
min_entities = 2
edge_types = ["duplicate_of"]

# uv-support — the astral-sh/uv public issue tracker, as the real problems behind the reports.
#
# Source shape (assumed): a JSONL export of the tracker, one record per tracker item —
# an issue's opening post, each comment, and each timeline event (labeled, assigned,
# closed, reopened, marked as duplicate, cross-referenced by a pull request). Every
# record carries the issue it belongs to, so a thread is one issue:
#   { "id": "...", "issue_number": "1234", "item": "comment", "title": "...",
#     "body": "...", "author": "login", "author_association": "MEMBER",
#     "created_at": "2025-03-01T12:00:00Z" }
# Timeline events are rendered to a sentence in `body` ("charliermarsh closed this as
# completed in #1250").

[corpus]
id = "uv-support"
name = "uv issue tracker (astral-sh/uv)"
description = "Issues, comments and maintainer actions on the uv issue tracker, extracted as the underlying problems behind reports: which reports are the same problem, what each problem is, where it shows up, where it stands and what was decided or shipped."
license = "private"
mesh_sharing = false
schema_version = 1

[acquire]
type = "local_file"
path = "SOURCE_PATH"

[extract]
type = "jsonl"
content_field = "body"
title_field = "title"

[chunk]
type = "paragraph"
max_chars = 2000
overlap_chars = 200

[index]
fts = true
vector = true

[enrichment]
enabled = true
type = "atlas"
domain = "uv-issue-tracker"

[enrichment.ontology]
version = 1
guidance = """
This is the public issue tracker of uv, the Python package and project manager Astral
builds in Rust. People open issues about crashes, wrong resolutions, slow installs,
platform quirks, how a command should behave, and features they want; maintainers label,
assign, link pull requests, close, reopen and mark duplicates. Many issues report the same
underlying problem in different words, on different uv versions, operating systems and
Python versions. Keep the issue (a report, known by its number) apart from the problem
(the real defect, gap or misunderstanding behind one or more reports). A report can start
as a question and turn out to be a bug, or start as a bug and turn out to be a
misunderstanding: what a problem is, is what the latest maintainer diagnosis says. Record
where each problem was seen (uv version, OS, architecture, Python version), what
maintainers decided about it, and which pull request and release shipped the change.
Error messages, tracebacks and version strings quoted in reports are evidence, not prose.
"""
must_not = [
  "say a problem is fixed, or fixed in a release, unless a maintainer or a merged pull request says so",
  "present a reporter's guess at the cause as the maintainers' diagnosis",
  "treat an issue closed as a duplicate as a resolved problem",
]

# ── Shape: the things ─────────────────────────────────────────────

[[enrichment.ontology.types]]
name = "issue"
kind = "entity"
label = "issue"
description = "One report on the tracker, known by its number: a bug report, question, feature request or discussion as the reporter filed it."
attributes = [
  { name = "number", type = "text", description = "The GitHub issue number, digits only." },
  { name = "title", type = "text" },
  { name = "filed_as", type = "text", values = ["bug", "question", "feature-request", "documentation", "performance", "other"], description = "What the reporter filed it as, not what it turned out to be." },
  { name = "opened", type = "time" },
]
identity = ["number"]
source = { metadata = ["issue_number"], attributes = { number = "value" } }

[[enrichment.ontology.types]]
name = "problem"
kind = "entity"
label = "problem"
description = "The real problem behind one or more issues: a defect, regression, performance problem, platform quirk, missing feature, documentation gap, or a misunderstanding of intended behaviour."
attributes = [
  { name = "summary", type = "text", description = "What the problem actually is, in one sentence." },
  { name = "component", type = "ref", of = "component" },
  { name = "nature", type = "text", values = ["bug", "regression", "performance", "platform-specific", "upstream", "missing-feature", "documentation-gap", "intended-behaviour", "user-error"] },
  { name = "error_signature", type = "text", description = "The characteristic error message or failure, normalised (paths, versions and usernames removed)." },
]
identity_criterion = "Two mentions are one problem when one change to uv (or one upstream fix) would resolve both: the same faulty behaviour of the same code path, however differently it was worded and whatever uv version, OS or Python version it was seen on. Same error message alone is not enough (one message can have several causes); different symptoms can be one problem when maintainers trace them to one cause. An issue marked as a duplicate of another reports the same problem."

# uv-support — recipe-author transcript

The partner wasn't available, so I answered each question from `DESCRIPTION.md` where it gives an answer
(source: **description**, with the words quoted). Where it doesn't, I answered from general knowledge of
GitHub issue tracking and of uv (source: **assumption**).

Closest shipped template: `product-support` (from `sovereign recipe new --ontology list`). I scaffolded it
for reference only. Its customer/feature/request shape doesn't fit an open-source tracker, so I wrote the
recipe from scratch.

## Source shape (opening question, before the interview)

**Q. What is the material, and in what form does it sit on disk?**
A. The astral-sh/uv GitHub issue tracker: issues, their comments, and maintainer actions. I assume a
local JSONL export with one record per tracker item: the opening post, each comment, and each timeline
event (labeled, assigned, closed, reopened, marked duplicate, cross-referenced by a PR). Each event is
rendered to a sentence in `body`. Every record carries `id`, `issue_number`, `item`, `title`, `body`,
`author`, `author_association` and `created_at`. So: `acquire.type = "local_file"`, `path = "SOURCE_PATH"`,
`extract.type = "jsonl"` (`content_field = "body"`, `title_field = "title"`), and a paragraph chunker.
Source: **description** for the content ("our public issue tracker on GitHub at astral-sh/uv. It holds
the issues people open, the comments on them, and what we as maintainers do with them: label, assign,
link to pull requests, close, reopen, mark as duplicates"). **Assumption** for the file format, the field
names, and that the `jsonl` extractor carries the non-content fields through as document metadata (the
`change.document` stamps and metadata `source`s depend on it).

## 1. Shape

**Q. What is this material about, and what would you want to know about each kind of thing? Is any of
them a kind of another, or a part something plays? Do you already have any of it in a table?**

A. The key distinction is between the *issue* (a report) and the *problem* (the real thing behind one
or more reports). Types:
- `issue` (entity). Attributes: number, title, filed_as (bug / question / feature-request / ...),
  opened. Instances come from the `issue_number` field of each record, with no model call.
- `problem` (entity). Attributes: summary, component, nature (bug, regression, performance,
  platform-specific, upstream, missing-feature, documentation-gap, intended-behaviour, user-error),
  error_signature.
- `component` (entity): the part of uv or the command a problem lives in.
- `package` (entity): a third-party package or index involved.
- `release` (entity): a uv version.
- `platform` (entity): OS / arch / detail.
- `python_build` (entity): implementation / version / provenance.
- `pull_request` (entity).
- `github_user` (entity, from the `author` field), plus the roles `maintainer` and `reporter`, each
  `role_of = "github_user"`.
- Relations: `reports` (issue→problem), `duplicate_of` (issue→issue), `addresses` (PR→problem),
  `shipped_in` (PR→release), `involves` (problem→package).
- Event: `triage_action` (actor = maintainer, on an issue: labeled / assigned / closed / reopened /
  marked-duplicate / linked-pr / ...).
- States: `issue_state` (of issue) and `problem_state` (of problem).
- No tables exist besides the tracker itself.

Source: **description**: "the real problems behind the reports"; "which issues are about the same
thing, what each one actually is, what versions and environments it shows up in"; "crashes, wrong
resolutions, slow installs, platform quirks, questions about how a command should behave, and feature
requests"; "different uv versions, operating systems and Python versions"; "label, assign, link to pull
requests, close, reopen, mark as duplicates". **Assumption** for: the component areas, `package`,
`python_build` provenance, and the maintainer/reporter roles.

## 2. Assertion

**Q. What do the sources say about those things — stating, requiring, deciding, asking? About what? How
do you tell strong evidence from weak? Who is speaking, and are they part of the subject? What must it
never do?**

A. All claims are about a `problem`, except decisions about how a command behaves, which are about a
`component`.
- `diagnosis` (assertive): what the problem is and why. Grades, strongest first: fix-merged,
  maintainer-reproduced, maintainer-assessment, reporter-reproduced, reporter-speculation.
- `occurrence` (assertive, labelled "sighting"): seen or not seen on a given uv version, platform and
  Python. Grades: maintainer-reproduced, reporter-reproduced-minimal, reporter-report, hearsay.
- `resolution` (declaration): fixed / wont-fix / intended-behaviour / upstream / duplicate /
  needs-reproduction / cannot-reproduce / reopened / stale, with the PR and the release it was fixed in.
- `behaviour_decision` (declaration, subject `component`): how a command should behave.
- `feature_request` (directive, request).
- `commitment` (commissive): will-fix / planned / pr-welcome / investigating.

Voices: maintainer, reporter, other-user, bot. Generic speaker references ("the reporter", "the original
poster", bots) never become entities.

must_not:
- Don't call something fixed without a maintainer or a merged PR saying so.
- Don't present a reporter's guess as the maintainers' diagnosis.
- Don't treat a duplicate closure as a resolution.

Source: **description**: "what each one actually is" (→ diagnosis); "what versions and environments it
shows up in" (→ occurrence); "what we decided or shipped about it" (→ resolution, behaviour_decision);
"questions about how a command should behave, and feature requests" (→ behaviour_decision,
feature_request). **Assumption** for: the grade scales, `commitment`, the voices, and the must_not
lines. I did not set `voices.self`: the partner is one maintainer among several, and their comments are
part of the subject matter.

## 3. Identity

**Q. How do you know two mentions are the same thing? Is there an ID?**

A.
- issue: issue number (external key).
- problem: no ID. Two mentions are one problem when one change to uv (or one upstream fix) would resolve
  both, regardless of wording, uv version, OS or Python version. A shared error message alone is not
  enough, and different symptoms traced to one cause are one problem. A maintainer duplicate marking means
  the same problem. This is written as `identity_criterion`, with no descriptive fallback.
- package: PEP 503 normalised name.
- release: version string.
- pull_request: repository + number.
- github_user / maintainer / reporter: login.
- component, platform, python_build: judged on descriptive keys.

Source: **description**: "many report the same underlying problem in different words, often across
different uv versions, operating systems and Python versions"; "mark as duplicates"; "which issues are
about the same thing". **Assumption** for: the one-fix criterion, the error-message caveat, and the
external keys (GitHub/PyPI conventions).

## 4. Change

**Q. When does a later statement replace an earlier one, and from when?**

A. A later `diagnosis` replaces an earlier one for the same problem: a question becomes a bug, or a bug
becomes a misunderstanding. The same goes for `resolution` (closed → reopened → fixed),
`behaviour_decision` and `commitment`. All of these supersede on the comment's date (`created_at` →
`document_date`). The thread is `issue_number` and the document id is the record `id`. `occurrence`
and `feature_request` accumulate rather than supersede. The issue and problem histories (`issue_state`,
`problem_state`, `triage_action`) record how each got where it is.

Source: **description**: "A report can start as a question and turn out to be a bug, or start as a bug
and turn out to be a misunderstanding"; "where it stands now and how it got there". **Assumption** for:
using comment time, not issue-open time, as the clock, and for which claim types accumulate.

## 5. Derivation

**Q. What should it notice that no single document says — contradictions, patterns, larger structures?
What looks like a contradiction but isn't?**

A. Look for tensions among diagnosis, occurrence, resolution and behaviour_decision on the same problem
(`same = ["subject"]`, not the default subject + clock, so a later sighting can contradict an earlier
fix). The main case is a problem declared fixed in release X and then seen again on a later version (a
regression or incomplete fix). Another is two maintainer decisions that disagree about a command.

Not conflicts:
- Different behaviour on different platforms or Python versions.
- Reclassification of a report (question ↔ bug).
- A sighting on a version older than the fix.
- A duplicate closed while the problem stays open.
- A reporter's guess that a maintainer later corrected.

Pattern: `circular_flow` over `duplicate_of` with min 2 (issues marked duplicates of each other).

The larger structure the user asked for (problem ← many issues) is carried by the `reports` relation
plus the problem identity criterion.

Source: **description**: "which issues are about the same thing ... where it stands now and how it got
there, and what we decided or shipped about it". **Assumption** for: the regression tension, the
not_conflicts list, and the duplicate-cycle pattern.

## Validation runs

### Run 1: `sovereign recipe validate recipe.toml`

  clock: document_date — supersession folds on document dates (the default; ...)
  tension selector: embedding top-k (k = 10, floor = 0.5) over diagnosis, occurrence, resolution, behaviour_decision — ...
  source: issue ← document fields issue_number (number: value) — one atom per identity value, ...
  identity: issue → number (external key, strict merge)
  identity: problem → RESOLVE under its identity_criterion, over the claims declaring it their subject; atoms Phase 1 named are retired

I wrote `recipe.toml` and `transcript.md`, and `sovereign recipe validate recipe.toml` passes. It passed on all three runs; I changed the recipe twice after reading the derived facets against my answers:
- **Run 1:** `maintainer` and `reporter` were matched on display name instead of GitHub login. I also removed a matching rule on `problem` that keyed on the error message, which contradicted my own rule that a shared error message isn't enough.
- **Run 2:** the corpus couldn't count sightings by OS or Python version, because those were plain text fields. I made them their own types (`platform`, `python_build`).

Run 3's facets all match the answers. The validator doesn't print the tension comparison rule or the duplicate-cycle pattern, so those two are untested. In the transcript, run 1's output is lightly trimmed and run 2 shows only the changed lines.

The recipe reads a local file at `SOURCE_PATH` with the `jsonl` extractor and a paragraph chunker. The ontology is version 1 under `type = "atlas"`.

**Types and how each is identified**

| Type | Kind | Identity |
|---|---|---|
| `issue` | entity, built from each record's `issue_number` | issue number (exact match) |
| `problem` | entity, the real problem behind one or more issues | no ID; two mentions are one problem when one change to uv (or one upstream fix) would resolve both, whatever the wording, version or platform. A shared error message alone isn't enough |
| `component` | entity | judged on area + command |
| `package` | entity | PEP 503 normalised name (exact) |
| `release` | entity | version (exact) |
| `pull_request` | entity | repository + number (exact) |
| `platform` | entity | judged on OS + architecture + detail |
| `python_build` | entity | judged on implementation + version + provenance |
| `github_user` | entity, built from each record's `author` | login (exact) |
| `maintainer`, `reporter` | roles a `github_user` plays | login (exact) |
| `reports`, `duplicate_of`, `addresses`, `shipped_in`, `involves` | relations | — |
| `triage_action` | event | — |
| `issue_state`, `problem_state` | states | — |
| `diagnosis`, `occurrence`, `resolution`, `behaviour_decision`, `feature_request`, `commitment` | claims | — |

A later `diagnosis`, `resolution`, `behaviour_decision` or `commitment` replaces an earlier one for the same problem, ordered by comment date. Contradictions are looked for among diagnoses, sightings, resolutions and decisions about the same problem. The main case is a problem declared fixed and then seen again on a later version.

**Assumptions I'm least sure of**
1. **The export format.** I assumed a JSONL file with one record per opening post, comment and timeline event, each carrying `id`, `issue_number`, `author` and `created_at`. I also assumed the `jsonl` extractor passes those extra fields through as document metadata. If it doesn't, the issue and user atoms and the per-comment dates (which order every replacement) produce nothing.
2. **Problem identity rests only on that written rule.** There's no fallback key. It matches the description, but how well problems get merged depends entirely on the model applying the rule.
3. **Comparing claims across time.** Contradictions are checked by problem only, not problem + date, so that a later sighting can contradict an earlier fix. That may also pair claims that were simply superseded; the list of things that aren't conflicts is meant to absorb that.
4. **Mostly my own invention:** the evidence-strength scales, the `commitment` type, the component areas, a decision about a command being about a `component` rather than a `problem`, and not marking the maintainers' voice as the owner's own (the person is one maintainer among several, so their comments are part of the subject).

I wrote `recipe.toml` and `transcript.md`, and `sovereign recipe validate recipe.toml` passes. It passed on all three runs; I changed the recipe twice after reading the derived facets against my answers:
- **Run 1:** `maintainer` and `reporter` were matched on display name instead of GitHub login. I also removed a matching rule on `problem` that keyed on the error message, which contradicted my own rule that a shared error message isn't enough.
- **Run 2:** the corpus couldn't count sightings by OS or Python version, because those were plain text fields. I made them their own types (`platform`, `python_build`).

Run 3's facets all match the answers. The validator doesn't print the tension comparison rule or the duplicate-cycle pattern, so those two are untested. In the transcript, run 1's output is lightly trimmed and run 2 shows only the changed lines.

The recipe reads a local file at `SOURCE_PATH` with the `jsonl` extractor and a paragraph chunker. The ontology is version 1 under `type = "atlas"`.

**Types and how each is identified**

| Type | Kind | Identity |
|---|---|---|
| `issue` | entity, built from each record's `issue_number` | issue number (exact match) |
| `problem` | entity, the real problem behind one or more issues | no ID; two mentions are one problem when one change to uv (or one upstream fix) would resolve both, whatever the wording, version or platform. A shared error message alone isn't enough |
| `component` | entity | judged on area + command |
| `package` | entity | PEP 503 normalised name (exact) |
| `release` | entity | version (exact) |
| `pull_request` | entity | repository + number (exact) |
| `platform` | entity | judged on OS + architecture + detail |
| `python_build` | entity | judged on implementation + version + provenance |
| `github_user` | entity, built from each record's `author` | login (exact) |
| `maintainer`, `reporter` | roles a `github_user` plays | login (exact) |
| `reports`, `duplicate_of`, `addresses`, `shipped_in`, `involves` | relations | — |
| `triage_action` | event | — |
| `issue_state`, `problem_state` | states | — |
| `diagnosis`, `occurrence`, `resolution`, `behaviour_decision`, `feature_request`, `commitment` | claims | — |

A later `diagnosis`, `resolution`, `behaviour_decision` or `commitment` replaces an earlier one for the same problem, ordered by comment date. Contradictions are looked for among diagnoses, sightings, resolutions and decisions about the same problem. The main case is a problem declared fixed and then seen again on a later version.

**Assumptions I'm least sure of**
1. **The export format.** I assumed a JSONL file with one record per opening post, comment and timeline event, each carrying `id`, `issue_number`, `author` and `created_at`. I also assumed the `jsonl` extractor passes those extra fields through as document metadata. If it doesn't, the issue and user atoms and the per-comment dates (which order every replacement) produce nothing.
2. **Problem identity rests only on that written rule.** There's no fallback key. It matches the description, but how well problems get merged depends entirely on the model applying the rule.
3. **Comparing claims across time.** Contradictions are checked by problem only, not problem + date, so that a later sighting can contradict an earlier fix. That may also pair claims that were simply superseded; the list of things that aren't conflicts is meant to absorb that.
4. **Mostly my own invention:** the evidence-strength scales, the `commitment` type, the component areas, a decision about a command being about a `component` rather than a `problem`, and not marking the maintainers' voice as the owner's own (the person is one maintainer among several, so their comments are part of the subject).

`scaffold-product-support.toml` is still in the directory. It's the closest template, which I generated for reference only, and my attempt to delete it was blocked by the permission system; you can delete it.
